data.title: Chieftains, princes and kings of the Slavic Veleti and Obodrites (Peter Šalkovský)
data.excerpt: The archaeologist Peter Šalkovský describes the elites of the Elbe Slavs for our portal: the Veleti, who had 95 strongholds and whose princes could be elected and deposed by the tribal assembly, and the Obodrites, whose last prince Pribislav became a prince of the Empire in 1170 while still feeling himself a Slav and an Obodrite. His descendants, the dukes and later grand dukes of Mecklenburg, remained leading princes of the German Empire until the end of the monarchy in 1918.
data.metaTitle: Šalkovský: chieftains and kings of the Veleti and Obodrites
data.metaDescription: The archaeologist Peter Šalkovský on the elites of the Elbe Slavs – the Veleti and the Obodrites – and their history east of the Elbe after 531.

keyFacts.label: Author
keyFacts.value: PhDr. Peter Šalkovský, DrSc. (Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences)

keyFacts.label: Territory
keyFacts.value: Western Pomerania, Mecklenburg, Holstein and Brandenburg (present-day north-eastern Germany)

timeline.title: The fall of the Thuringian kingdom
timeline.description: After the fall of the Thuringian kingdom, only individual groups of the Germanic Saxons and Thuringians remained in the territory east of the Elbe and the Saale, which later made occupation by the Slavs possible.

timeline.title: Civitas Dragaviti
timeline.description: The first Slavic stronghold documented in writing in present-day north-eastern Germany, the seat of the Veletian prince Dragovit, is mentioned in the Annals of the Frankish Empire. In the same year the Veletian tribal confederation succumbed to a campaign by Charlemagne supported by the Obodrites.

timeline.title: The death of Prince Dražko
timeline.description: The Obodrite prince Dražko, who extended the confederation from the mouth of the Havel as far as the North Sea, died a violent death.

timeline.title: Prince Ljub
timeline.description: The Annals of the Kingdom of the Franks recorded Prince Ljub (Liub) among the Veleti; he fell in the war against the Obodrites.

timeline.title: The campaign of Louis the German
timeline.description: After the death of the chief Obodrite prince Gostomysl, Emperor Louis the German divided the territory among the four main Obodrite tribes headed by their own princes.

timeline.title: The suppression of Stoignev’s uprising
timeline.description: The uprising of the Obodrite magnate Stoignev was suppressed.

timeline.title: The great revolt of the Wilzi
timeline.description: The revolt of the pagan Wilzi (from then on called the Lutici) brought both the renewal of their tribal confederation and independence for the Slavic territories east of the Elbe from the Kingdom of Germany for almost 200 years. The Obodrites joined the uprising as well.

timeline.title: The expulsion of Prince Mstivoj
timeline.description: The Obodrite prince Mstivoj (Mstislav) was expelled when he attempted Christianisation.

timeline.title: Internal struggles of the Lutici
timeline.description: Internal conflicts and bloody struggles for power among the main tribes of the Wilzian confederation (the Redarians, the Circipani and the Kessini), culminating in 1056–1057, marked the beginning of the demise of the Lutician tribal confederation.

timeline.title: The murder of Prince Gottschalk
timeline.description: The Nakonid prince Gottschalk was murdered by pagan rebels in the stronghold of Lenzen.

timeline.title: The division of rule between Pribislav and Niklot
timeline.description: Pribislav, the son of the Obodrite prince Budivoj, and his relative Niklot divided the rule according to territories – Pribislav received the land of the Wagrians and the Polabians, while Niklot ruled in the land of the Obodrites.

timeline.title: The destruction of the stronghold of Alt Lübeck
timeline.description: The stronghold of Alt Lübeck (Liubice) was destroyed by the Rugians.

timeline.title: The fall of Starigard
timeline.description: Starigard (Oldenburg) lost its political importance when it was captured and devastated by the Danes, and its massive Saxon colonisation began.

timeline.title: The battle of Verchen
timeline.description: After losing the battle of Verchen, the last Obodrite prince Pribislav became a Christian and a vassal of the Saxon prince Henry the Lion.

timeline.title: The fall of Arkona
timeline.description: The tribe of the Rani on the island of Rügen finally succumbed to the Danes; the central stronghold of Arkona was captured, plundered and burnt down.

timeline.title: Pribislav becomes a prince of the Empire
timeline.description: Pribislav became a prince of the Empire, while continuing to feel himself a Slav and an Obodrite.

timeline.title: The death of Prince Pribislav
timeline.description: Pribislav of Mecklenburg, prince of the Slavs, the last king of the Obodrites and Christian patron of Mecklenburg, died.

timeline.title: The end of the Mecklenburg monarchy
timeline.description: Pribislav’s descendants, the dukes and later grand dukes of Mecklenburg, were leading princes of the German Empire until the end of the monarchy in this year.

children.text: The archaeologist Peter Šalkovský has written the following interesting article on the history of the Slavs in Germany for our portal:

After the fall of the Thuringian kingdom in 531, only individual groups of the Germanic Saxons and Thuringians remained in the territory east of the Elbe and the Saale. Subsequently, until the end of the 6th century AD, this territory probably became no man’s land in terms of power, which was also reflected in the lack of interest shown by contemporary early medieval authors. And it was probably only at this time that the Slavs from the Bohemian Elbe region could begin to move further into the vacated space along the Elbe, the Saale and the Havel as far as central Germany. Because of the shortage of finds, we do not yet know more precisely when this happened.

In the territory of Saxony and eastern Thuringia between the Saale and the Elbe, the beginning of Slavic occupation by the Slavic culture known as the Prague-type culture is placed at the end of the 6th century and in the first half of the 7th century. The remainder of the eastern parts of present-day Germany, roughly as far as the Elbe, and its north – Western Pomerania as far as Rügen and eastern Holstein – was occupied somewhat later, gradually in several waves, mainly from the north-west, by the early Slavic Sukow-Dziedzice culture, which was probably a regional northern derivation of the Prague-type culture and from which the individual Pomeranian, Veletian-Lutician and Obodrite tribes “developed” in the course of the 8th and 9th centuries.

In the period from the 9th to the 11th century, more than 70 tribal territories and small tribes are mentioned by name in various charters and chronicles in the territories of the north-western Slavs.

The Veletian tribal confederation, which was settled in the area of southern Western Pomerania, the eastern part of Mecklenburg and the north of Brandenburg, had a strong central government by the second half of the 8th century at the latest. It was headed by Prince Dragovit. His seat, known as Civitas Dragaviti, the very first Slavic stronghold documented in writing in present-day north-eastern Germany, mentioned in 789 in the Annals of the Frankish Empire, is usually identified with the site of Vorwerk-Alte Schanze near Demmin in Western Pomerania, which covers about 2.5 ha. In 789 the Wilzian (Veletian) tribal confederation succumbed to a campaign by Charlemagne supported by the Obodrites. This defeat weakened the central Wilzian government so much that the individual tribes of the confederation became independent, or rather lived for almost a hundred years in a tributary relationship to the East Frankish Empire.

children.text: According to the Bavarian Geographer, the Veleti (Uuilci Wieleten), also referred to as the Wilzi (Wilzen, Vuilci), had 95 strongholds and four tribal territories in the 9th century. They were governed by an assembly made up of the representatives of the four basic tribes around the river Peene. The main Veletian tribes were the Redarians (Ratari, Redarii), the Circipani (Circipanen), the Kessini (Kessinen) and the Tollensians (Tollensanen).

The Annals of the Kingdom of the Franks recorded for the year 823 that a certain rex Wilzorum by the name of Ljub (Liub) ruled among the Veleti and fell in the war against the Obodrites. Ljub apparently ruled one of the Veletian regiones and, at the time of the war with the Obodrites, held the office of supreme military commander. Ljub evidently enjoyed high respect that persisted even after his death, which resulted in the election of his eldest son Milogast by the tribal assembly (populus Wilzorum). Milogast, perhaps not as capable as his father, was deposed a few months after his election by the tribal assembly because he “exercised his rule inappropriately”, and his place was taken, by the will of the assembly, by his younger brother Čedodrag.

For the rest of the 9th century, the dark century of Veletian history, the central princely power disappeared and the princes were markedly weakened; the written sources tell us nothing more about them. The tribal assembly regained importance, and above all the college of pagan priests, which in this time of crisis won great influence over the running of the whole confederation. The princes of the individual regiones were either eliminated in the course of the second half of the 9th century, or were left with only an insignificant fraction of power in matters concerning the whole confederation. The new political order of the Veletian confederation was based on joint assemblies of the representatives of the priests of the individual civitates and regiones. The priestly college maintained its influence through an extensive network of pagan temples in the individual tribal districts, which paid regular dues to Rethra. Although the Veleti had many, and very large, strongholds (Feldberg, Liepen, Neu Niekör, Sternberger Burg, Sukow, Vorwerk, Wildberg and Kastorf and others), they probably had no main princely ruling centre, or rather it was formed by the pagan sanctuary at Rethra (Riedigost). After its demise the centre shifted to the stronghold of Arkona with the monumental temple of the god Svantovít on the island of Rügen.

It was only the great revolt of the still pagan Wilzi in 983, after which they began to be called the Lutici, that brought not only the renewal of their tribal confederation, but also independence for the Slavic territories east of the Elbe from the Kingdom of Germany for a long period lasting almost 200 years. The Wilzian confederation, which had provoked the revolt, rose from the ruins and in the 11th century became a significant military force in the north of Central Europe. Internal conflicts and bloody struggles for power among the main tribes of the confederation, the Redarians, the Circipani and the Kessini, culminating in 1056–1057, marked the beginning of the demise of the Lutician tribal confederation, of its fragmentation, of its gradual domination by the Obodrites and the Saxon dukes, and of its assimilation by German immigrants.

children.text: The tribe of the Rani, the Rugians, who lived north of the Veleti on the island of Rügen in northern Germany, also long professed the pagan religion. They resisted repeated attempts at war, above all by the Danes, until they finally succumbed to them in 1168. The central stronghold of Arkona was captured, plundered and burnt down. The tribal rulers of the time, Jaromar I and Teslaw, who had their seat in the stronghold at nearby Charenza (Garz, Venz?), surrendered to the Danish king Valdemar after the fall of Arkona and became his vassals until 1325 (Wisław III). Later they were dependent on the West Pomeranian German duchy, into which they were incorporated after the death of Warcisław X (1478). In the course of three centuries the Slavic Rugians were not only completely Christianised, but also assimilated by the newly settled German population.
The Obodrites

We probably have the most written information about the Obodrite tribal confederation, which arose in western Mecklenburg and south-eastern Holstein, that is, west of the Wilzian confederation, probably as early as the 8th century, out of various small tribes unknown by name but evidently of related origin, which were headed by their own chieftains or – as the Frankish sources put it – petty kings (regulus). From among these they elected and appointed the chief leader of the confederation, a prince sometimes also called king, who took decisions with the consent of the assembly. The confederation, which in the field of foreign policy was sometimes also divided into western and eastern Obodrites, did not have sovereignty, because the small tribes on the coast of the Baltic Sea had independent relations with the Scandinavian world, especially with the Danes. The remaining territories under the rule of the confederation’s prince Vlčan (Witzan) were, by 780 at the latest, vassals of the Franks and their allies against the Saxons, who were still pagan at that time. Probably the other Obodrite princes Dražko (Drasco), Slavomír (Sclaomir) and Sedrag (Ceadrag) were also elected, or rather installed, with the support of the Frankish rulers, and their task was to control the territories on the right bank of the Elbe east of the border of the Frankish Empire. The Obodrite confederation reached its greatest extent, stretching from the mouth of the Havel as far as the North Sea, under the rule of Vlčan’s son Dražko (795/804–810), when he also sought to annex the territories and ports then controlled by the Danes. In the service of the Franks he kept the still pagan Saxons and the Danes in check for years, until his violent death in 810. Goidelaib is mentioned as an example of one of the lesser princes under Dražko’s rule. These princes are said to have ruled in the individual princely districts, two of which were controlled by Goidelaib.

These Obodrite princes too must already have had seats similar to those of their contemporary, the Veletian Dragovit mentioned above (Civitas Dragaviti, 789). We know that the large central strongholds such as Oldenburg, Mecklenburg, Hitzacker and others lying in the Obodrite sphere have their beginnings, at least according to the classic dating, as early as the 8th century. However, the first few dendrochronological investigations date some of them somewhat later (for example Alt Lübeck to 818, Scharstorf to 835, Bosau to 837 and Ilow to 840). Other important strongholds of the Obodrites were the later strongholds of Ilow, Dobin on Lake Schwerin and Friedrichsrühe near Parchim.

In the 9th century the Obodrite confederation (Nortabtrezi) is said, according to the Bavarian Geographer, to have had a total of 53 strongholds in four territories. At various times from the 8th to the 12th century its members were, besides the Obodrites themselves in the narrower sense between the Bay of Wismar and Lake Schwerin, also the Wagrians, who were settled furthest to the west in what is now eastern Holstein. Also the Polabians, who separated from the Wagrians in the 11th century, then the Warnabi, settled to the east on the upper course of the Warnow, and finally the Drevani (Travunjani), settled further south along the Elbe. As satellite tribes outside the Obodrite settlement territory, or rather to the south and east of it, the Linones also belonged to them temporarily, as did other smaller tribes, and in certain periods the Kessini, the Circipani and the Morizani, who were at times also linked with the Veleti.

children.text: The positive relations of the Franks towards the Obodrites ended after their attempts (under the rule of Dražko’s brother Slavomír and his son Sedrag) at an alliance with the Danes against the Frankish Empire. The centralising development of the Obodrite confederation was halted for a longer time by further campaigns of Emperor Louis the German around 844, who, after the death of its chief prince Gostomysl, divided the territory among the four main Obodrite tribes headed by their own princes.

A century later, despite the changing situation and their tributary dependence on the empire, the Obodrites grew strong again. In 955 another uprising, led by the Obodrite magnate Stoignev, was suppressed. It was only in 983, when they joined the Lutician uprising against the Germans and against Christianisation, that they also gained independence for a long time. Individual members of the ruling families, however, alternately attempted a renewed Christianisation – like Prince Mstivoj (Mstislav), who was expelled later, in 1018 – as well as cooperation with the German state or, conversely, a revitalisation of the pagan cult.

In the 10th century we learn about the main parts of this new Obodrite formation. These were the tribes of the Wagrians and the Polabians, representing newly separated groups from the former great tribe, and the Obodrites themselves, who were evidently still ruled by the same princely family or its distant relatives. These three units formed the tribal core, but their internal composition was not the same. Among the two “younger tribes” the older tribal structure survived, in which the rule of princes (Principes Sclavorum), some of whom we even know by name, alternated irregularly with tribal assemblies.

Among the Obodrites, by contrast, who represented the core of the former great tribe in the area of Mecklenburg, princely power was strengthened and the tribal assembly was eliminated, being replaced by an assembly of the most powerful individuals, who headed the lower tribal units (nobiles, sociis) and formed the great princely retinue. The inner circle of this retinue represented the prince’s closest entourage, and his position rested, among other things, precisely on their loyalty.

children.text: The seat of what is perhaps the best-known Obodrite dynasty, the Nakonids, who from the 10th century onwards sought for a century (with interruptions) to found a state of their own, and the main bastion of the Obodrites, was the stronghold at Dorf Mecklenburg, probably originally called Veligrad or Michelsburg. Besides the words of Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, who describes it as Nakon’s stronghold, comparable with the princely strongholds of the Bulgarians or the Poles, its exceptional position is also confirmed by the archaeological finds.

One of the best-known Nakonid princes was Gottschalk, known for his alternating inclination towards paganism and towards Christianity; he was murdered in 1066 by pagan rebels in the stronghold of Lenzen.

The centre of the Wagrians, in turn, was the well-known Starigard (Oldenburg). Although it was burnt down several times, it functioned until the 12th century and its internal layout was then comparable with that of contemporary Carolingian strongholds. Starigard lost its political importance in 1149, when it was captured and devastated by the Danes and its massive Saxon colonisation began. At the beginning of the 13th century the ruins of the Slavic stronghold were rebuilt into a new seat of the counts of Holstein, and the settlement below it was granted town privileges.

Alt Lübeck (Liubice), also an important Obodrite stronghold, became in the middle of the 11th century the residential town of the last Obodrite Nakonid princes. It was rebuilt, enlarged, and on the initiative of Prince Gottschalk a large building complex arose here. The flowering of the stronghold continued under the Obodrite “king” Heinrich of Alt Lübeck, when it acquired an urban character and consisted of the stronghold, a port and three baileys. In 1138 the stronghold was destroyed by the Rugians. Its name Liubice was transferred to the port town founded on a nearby island, out of which today’s Lübeck grew.

At the beginning of the 1130s, probably in 1131, Pribislav, the son of the Obodrite prince Budivoj, and Niklot, probably his uncle or a close relative, divided the rule (principatus) not according to tribes, but according to their territories. Pribislav received the land (provinciam) of the Wagrians and the Polabians, and Niklot ruled in the land of the Obodrites. The object of the division was thus not the people, but their lands. Niklot was subsequently described by Helmold, besides the traditional title “princeps Obotritorum or princeps Slavorum”, also in connection with the land of the Obodrites as “Niclotus princeps terrae Obotritorum”. Today he not only has a monumental equestrian statue, erected in 1855 on the front façade of the castle in Schwerin, but his name is also borne by a beer, “Fürst Niklot – Premium Quality”.

The central Obodrite stronghold of Mecklenburg, covering 1.4 ha and encircled by a very massive timber-and-earth rampart, was destroyed after the initially successful wars against the German and Danish feudal lords in 1147–1164. Although it gave its name to today’s land of Mecklenburg, it is now the village of Dorf Mecklenburg. A similar fate also befell other Obodrite strongholds, among them Behren-Lübchin in 1171; not even the efforts at Christianisation on the part of a section of the Obodrite ruling class were of any help.

In the second half of the 12th century the Obodrite tribal confederation too finally succumbed to the attacks of the Saxon dukes. After losing the battle of Verchen in 1164, the last Obodrite prince Pribislav became a Christian and a vassal of the Saxon prince Henry the Lion, and received a large part of his former principality as the fief Terra Obodritorum.

children.text: In 1170 he became a prince of the Empire. He nevertheless continued to feel himself a Slav and an Obodrite, as did his immediate successors, which is also attested by written records of the names of the loyal magnates with whom they surrounded themselves – Sirizlaf, Wolcowitz, Wartiz, Bizpraw, Radomir, Chubanze, Veneiko, Woiwoto, Damascho, Paliz, Gusiz, Zlauteich, Chemko, Dursico, Janeke, Stoislav, Dargatz, Jarozlav and others.

Practically throughout the whole period under consideration, from the end of the 9th to the end of the 12th century, the Obodrite princes were titled not only with terms such as dux Obotritorum or princeps Obotritorum, but also as dux Slavis, princeps Slavorum or princeps Winulorum.

After 1200 an intensive colonisation by German settlers from Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Friesland and Holstein began in Mecklenburg, in the course of which most of the Mecklenburg towns were founded. The late medieval territorial and administrative division of the land, the organisation of the so-called stronghold wardenships – Burgwarde – that is, of territories administered by a warden as the plenipotentiary of the prince or king in a centre with a stronghold, was based, at least in the Obodrite and Lutician territories of eastern Holstein, Lauenburg, Mecklenburg and Western Pomerania, on the older division into the old Slavic stronghold districts (civitates, Burgbezirke) and the late Obodrite and late Lutician principalities and castellanies of the 11th–12th centuries.

Although the dynasty of the Obodrite princes did not attain, at least not in full measure, the position of hereditary rulers with the exclusive right to supreme power that the Přemyslids or the Piasts enjoyed, by its power and influence it managed to win back its lost positions several times. Pribislav’s descendants, the dukes and later also the grand dukes of Mecklenburg, were leading princes and figures of the German Empire until the end of the monarchy in 1918, and their Obodrite “royal” origin was long emphasised in the chronicles. The Mecklenburg dynasty has a monumental memorial preserved in the main Protestant church in Bad Doberan in Mecklenburg, where the tombs and the tombstone of the Mecklenburg rulers from Pribislav to Heinrich Borwin II are placed. Heinrich Borwin II (1219–1226), prince of Mecklenburg, lord of Rostock and founder of the town of Güstrow, had a statue erected here by Borwin’s well as early as 1889. We can only regret that we Slovaks have almost no memorials to “our” famous men (counts, princes, kings, but also artists, scholars, generals and so on) who lived and worked between the Danube and the Tatras, through which we might express our respect and symbolic gratitude to them – regardless of whether they felt themselves to be Slovaks, Hungarians or Germans, whether they spoke the Slovak language, or fought on the opposing side (as did most of the Elbe and Pomeranian chieftains and princes), or even, like Prince Niklot, fell in battle as our opponents.
PhDr. Peter Šalkovský, DrSc., Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences.
